summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults is legal in Madagascar, but only from age 21. Penal Code Article 331 treats same-sex acts involving a person under 21 as indecent assault, with a reported penalty band of five to ten years' imprisonment, so the age of consent is unequal and a visitor whose partner or counterparty is under 21 faces a serious criminal exposure that a heterosexual visitor does not.

Marriage is closed to same-sex couples. Article 2 of Law No. 2007-022 on Marriage and Matrimonial Regimes prohibits marriage between two persons of the same sex, whether before the Civil Registrar or under traditional ceremonies. Article 39 of the same law names gender identity as a cause for absolute nullity of marriage, which is a direct legal exposure for a trans visitor whose relationship status is examined locally.

Status on arrival is thin. There is no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, no anti-discrimination law, and no legal gender recognition, so a trans traveller holds no locally recognised identity, no partner status and no named protection under Malagasy law.

The social environment is the dominant practical factor. Homosexuality is not illegal, yet it is widely considered socially unacceptable, and LGBT Malagasy people conceal their lives in order to keep jobs and live in peace, maintaining private networks and coded language, according to a France 24 report on the country. A trans visitor who is read locally as gender-nonconforming should expect the same pressure to stay invisible, and should not assume that lawful conduct will be met with tolerance.

Documented hostility is directed hardest at transgender people. The United States State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report for Madagascar recorded societal discrimination and violence against the LGBT community, with public attitudes ranging from tacit acceptance to violent rejection, particularly of transgender sex workers, who were frequent targets of verbal abuse, stone throwing and even murder. Supporters of a same-sex couple were subjected to insults and death threats on social media, and religious leaders publicly accused them of "promising homosexuality".

Public expression is constrained. In early July 2021 the Malagasy government cancelled an LGBTQ party held at a bar in Antananarivo on the grounds of "incitement to debauchery". A visitor who attends, organises or is publicly associated with an LGBT event risks comparable police intervention regardless of the absence of a general sodomy offence.

Access to care is governed mainly by HIV policy. Act No. 2005-040 on the Fight against HIV/AIDS requires information, education and communication programmes adapted to the sexual orientation of target groups, and Article 26 mandates special provisions protecting men who have sex with men, sex workers, young people and mobile populations against HIV transmission. Care-seeking is complicated by documented conversion-therapy approaches offered to LGBT people by religious leaders, and by the violent rejection of transgender people recorded in the 2011 reporting.
tangentialFactors:
Madagascar sits outside the regional trend toward decriminalisation: as of July 2020 roughly 22 of 53 African states had moved to decriminalise same-sex conduct, and Madagascar's position is partial rather than aligned with either camp, since conduct is lawful only above age 21 and every adjacent civic right remains closed.

State protection capacity is weak and was weak at the point the best-documented reporting was produced. The 2011 Human Rights Report covers a post-coup regime and records unlawful killings alongside societal discrimination and violence against women, persons with disabilities and the LGBT community, which indicates a general pattern of discrimination rather than an isolated anti-LGBT posture, and suggests that official recourse after an incident is unlikely to be effective.

The government's current official position was tested in January 2025 during its fourth Universal Periodic Review, in which 235 recommendations were considered. The government rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent. Six Malagasy organisations, including Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers'Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+, publicly stated that refusing to act endorses impunity and condones violence, which sets the expectation that the legal position will not improve during a near-term visit.
localsOnly:
Family formation is restricted to heterosexual married couples. Article 33 of Law No. 2005-014 on Adoption states that full adoption is only permitted to heterosexual spouses, and the same exclusion governs custody, so an LGBT resident has no route to legally recognised parenthood through adoption.

Data protection offers residents a partial shield. Law No. 2014-038 on the Protection of Personal Data, Article 18, bars processing of sensitive data including data on health or sexual life, and Law No. 2017-045 on Credit Information Bureaus, Article 2, treats sexual orientation as sensitive data.

Residents who are outed face both legal and social consequences. In a 2020 case a 33-year-old woman was arrested for the statutory rape of a 19-year-old woman after the younger woman's mother filed a complaint, with the mother allegedly acting to cover up an incest and rape accusation against the father; the 19-year-old was the subject of a charge under the Penal Code's indecent-acts provision carrying a reported two-to-five-year penalty. Religious leaders subsequently offered the young woman conversion therapy.

With no anti-discrimination statute in force, residents have no statutory complaint mechanism for the discrimination documented in official reporting. Organised advocacy exists and is vocal: the six organisations named at the January 2025 Universal Periodic Review include Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers'Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage and Madagascar LGBT+, and LGBT Malagasy people run their own networks and coded language to hold employment and live undisturbed.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources disagree on the penalty band that Article 331 carries for same-sex acts involving a person under 21: one inventory source gives five to ten years' imprisonment for the under-21 indecent-assault band, while another gives two to five years for "indecent or against nature" acts. The discrepancy is unresolved here and should be checked against the current consolidated Penal Code text before the figure is relied on.

Not sourced: whether Article 331 is applied to female same-sex conduct as well as male, whether any legal gender recognition procedure exists in practice despite the absence of a statute, and whether a passport or identity document carrying a gender marker inconsistent with presentation triggers additional screening on arrival or at immigration. Entry and visa rules specific to trans travellers are not covered by the available inventory.

The France 24 report on concealment is cited in one place as August 2024 while its published URL indicates 8 April 2024; the date discrepancy is unresolved. The 2011 Human Rights Report evidence on violence is more than a decade old, and no more recent official country report in the inventory documents present-day incidence or police response.
